q: What is the most important prognostic factor for cutaneous melanoma without distant metastasis?
a: Breslow depth (vertical thickness of the lesion measured in millimeters from the granular layer of the epidermis).

q: Differentiate Pemphigus Vulgaris from Bullous Pemphigoid regarding autoantibodies, Nikolsky sign, and mucous membrane involvement.
a:
• Pemphigus Vulgaris: IgG against desmoglein-1/3; Nikolsky (+); oral mucosal involvement common; flaccid blisters.
• Bullous Pemphigoid: IgG against hemidesmosomes (BP180/BP230); Nikolsky (-); mucosal involvement rare; tense blisters.

q: What body surface area (BSA) cutoff differentiates Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) from Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)?
a:
• SJS: <10% BSA detachment.
• SJS/TEN overlap: 10%–30% BSA detachment.
• TEN: >30% BSA detachment.

q: What premalignant lesion presents as rough, scaly, sandpaper-like macules/papules on sun-exposed skin, and what is the first-line topical treatment for widespread disease?
a: Actinic Keratosis (precursor to Squamous Cell Carcinoma). First-line topical treatment for widespread field cancerization is 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) cream or imiquimod.

q: What is the characteristic clinical presentation and histologic finding of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)?
a:
Clinical: Pearly, translucent papule/nodule with telangiectasias and rolled borders ± central ulceration.
Histology: Nests of basaloid epithelial cells with peripheral palisading nuclei.

q: What is the stepwise escalating pharmacotherapy for Acne Vulgaris from mild to severe refractory nodulocystic disease?
a:
1. Mild: Topical retinoids ± benzoyl peroxide.
2. Moderate: Add topical antibiotics (clindamycin/erythromycin) or oral tetracyclines (doxycycline/minocycline).
3. Severe/Nodulocystic: Oral isotretinoin (requires negative pregnancy tests and enrollment in iPLEDGE due to severe teratogenicity).

q: What chronic inflammatory dermatosis presents with recurrent, painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in intertriginous areas (axillae, groin)? What biological agent is approved for moderate-to-severe disease?
a: Hidradenitis Suppurativa (follicular occlusion disease). First-line biologic is an anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody (e.g., adalimumab).

q: What is the diagnosis for silvery-white plaques on extensor surfaces displaying the Auspitz sign, and which cytokine pathways are key targets for modern systemic therapy?
a: Psoriasis Vulgaris (Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding upon scale removal). Targeted biologics include anti-IL-17 (e.g., secukinumab), anti-IL-12/23 (e.g., ustekinumab), or anti-TNF-α inhibitors.

q: What key genetic mutation (epidermal barrier protein) is strongly associated with Atopic Dermatitis, and what non-steroidal topical class is used for facial lesions?
a: Inactivating mutations in the Filaggrin (FLG) gene. Facial/intertriginous flare-ups are treated with topical calcineurin inhibitors (e.g., tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) to avoid steroid-induced skin atrophy.

q: What greasy, erythematous rash with yellow scales affecting the scalp and nasolabial folds is associated with Malassezia fungi, and which underlying neurological condition is classic for severe recalcitrant presentations?
a: Seborrheic Dermatitis. Strongly associated with Parkinson disease (and HIV infection).

q: A patient with chronic Hepatitis C presents with painless blisters, skin fragility, and hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed hands. What enzyme deficiency causes this condition, and what accumulates in the urine?
a: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT) due to deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD). Urinalysis demonstrates elevated uroporphyrins (turns tea-colored or fluoresces coral red under Wood lamp).

q: What chronic facial dermatosis presents with central facial erythema, telangiectasias, and pustules triggered by alcohol, heat, or spicy foods, and what topical antimicrobial is first-line?
a: Rosacea (papulopustular variant). First-line topical treatments include metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin. (Note: lack of comedones distinguishes it from acne vulgaris).

q: What auto-inflammatory skin disease presents with pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules and plaques with fine white lines (Wickham striae), and which chronic viral infection should be screened for?
a: Lichen Planus (the 5 Ps: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar Papules/Plaques). Strong association with Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.

q: An adult with chronic diarrhea presents with intensely pruritic, grouped papulovesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. What is the diagnosis, autoantibody target, and acute medical treatment?
a: Dermatitis Herpetiformis associated with Celiac Disease (IgA anti-epidermal transglutaminase deposits at dermal papillae tips). Acute treatment is dapsone; long-term management requires a strict gluten-free diet.

q: What condition presents as painful, erythematous, non-ulcerative nodular lesions on the anterior lower legs (shins), and what are 3 major high-yield underlying etiologies?
a: Erythema Nodosum (panniculitis). High-yield causes include: Streptococcal pharyngitis, Sarcoidosis, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), Histoplasmosis, and Tuberculosis.

q: A patient with Ulcerative Colitis develops a rapidly expanding, extremely painful skin ulcer with violaceous, undermined borders after minor skin trauma. What is the diagnosis and primary management?
a: Pyoderma Gangrenosum (demonstrates pathergy). Management involves systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressants (e.g., cyclosporine, infliximab). Do NOT perform surgical debridement as it worsens the ulcer.

q: What skin manifestation presents as hyperpigmented, velvety plaques in intertriginous zones (neck, axillae), and what are the two main clinical associations (benign vs malignant)?
a:
Acanthosis Nigricans.
• Benign: Insulin resistance (Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, PCOS, obesity).
• Malignant: Gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma (especially gastric adenocarcinoma).

q: What is the Leser-Trélat sign and what underlying pathology does it indicate?
a: The sudden eruption of multiple seborrheic keratoses within a short period. It serves as a paraneoplastic marker for underlying internal malignancy, most commonly gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.

q: A patient started on allopurinol 4 weeks ago presents with fever, widespread maculopapular rash, facial edema, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count >1,500/μL). What is the diagnosis?
a: DRESS Syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms). Caused by drugs like antiepileptics (phenytoin, carbamazepine), allopurinol, or antibiotics (vancomycin). Visceral organ involvement (e.g., hepatitis, interstitial nephritis) is common.

q: What skin infection presents with small, firm, umbilicated dome-shaped papules with a central curd-like core, and when seen extensively in an adult, warrants testing for which underlying condition?
a: Molluscum Contagiosum (caused by Poxvirus). In adults with widespread or facial lesions, screening for HIV infection (immunocompromised state) is mandatory.
